# SealManifest

Namespace `Nfty.Core.Publish` in assembly `Nfty.Core`.

```csharp
public record SealManifest : ISchemaVersioned
```

The `seal.json` at the top of a sealed export — **plaintext, deliberately**.

## Remarks

**Why any of it is readable without the key.** A recipient holding a file they cannot open needs to be told what it is, or the only thing the format communicates is "something went wrong". `inspect` prints this header, so they learn the collection's name, its size, and the note the author wrote them, and then know which passphrase to go and find.

**That is a deliberate metadata leak and it is the whole cost of the choice.** Anyone who obtains the file learns that the collection exists, what it is called and how large it is. The art, the traits, the rarity and the DNA are all inside the encryption; the label on the tin is not.

[`SealManifest.AuthenticationVersion`](Nfty.Core.Publish.SealManifest.md#p-authenticationversion) 2 binds fields unambiguously. Legacy version 1 remains readable with its original delimiter encoding; its collection/count/note labels cannot be made retroactively tamper-proof. New writers always emit version 2.

**[`SealManifest.PolicyMac`](Nfty.Core.Publish.SealManifest.md#p-policymac) authenticates the header.** It is an HMAC over [`SealManifest.Canonical()`](Nfty.Core.Publish.SealManifest.md#m-canonical) keyed by a second key derived from the same passphrase, so someone who intercepts the file cannot edit `allowExport` to true, or restate the note, and pass it on. Someone who HAS the passphrase can recompute it — that is not a gap in the implementation, it is what it means to hold the key, and it is why the seal is described everywhere in this product as a lock on a door rather than a wall.

```csharp
public SealManifest(string SealId, string Collection, int Count, string? Note, SealPolicy Policy, string PolicyMac, SealKdf Kdf, SealCipher Cipher, int SchemaVersion = 2);
```

**Parameters**

- `SealId` (`string`) - A random 128-bit id, hex. It is in the AAD of every frame, so frames cannot be spliced between two files sealed with the same passphrase.
- `Collection` (`string`) - The collection's name, for a recipient with no key.
- `Count` (`int`) - How many assets are inside.
- `Note` (`string?`) - What the author wants the recipient to read first. Null when none was given.
- `Policy` (`SealPolicy`) - What nfty will let the recipient do.
- `PolicyMac` (`string`) - Hex HMAC-SHA256 over [`SealManifest.Canonical()`](Nfty.Core.Publish.SealManifest.md#m-canonical).
- `Kdf` (`SealKdf`) - How the key was derived.
- `Cipher` (`SealCipher`) - How the payload was encrypted.
- `SchemaVersion` (`int`) - The schema this header was written against.

## Methods

### Canonical() { #m-canonical }

```csharp
public string Canonical();
```

The exact UTF-8 text the MAC covers.

**Returns.** Fields in a fixed order, using the declared authentication version.

**Exceptions**

- [`SealedSetException`](Nfty.Core.Publish.SealedSetException.md) - The authentication version is unsupported.

**Remarks**

**Spelled out by hand rather than by re-serializing this record**, because the MAC has to mean the same thing in every future build. `System.Text.Json` emits a record's members in declaration order, so MACing its own JSON would make reordering two properties — a refactor with no observable effect anywhere else — silently invalidate every seal ever written. This method is the format; the record is just how it is carried.
